title: Physical Conditions of Habitats
seo_title: Year 6 Science: Physical Conditions of Habitats Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Investigate the physical conditions of a habitat and analyse how the growth and survival of living things is affected by changing physical conditions (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 6 science worksheets on the physical conditions of habitats: temperature, water, light, soil and salt, and how drought, heat and salinity affect Australian plants and animals. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Physical conditions affect growth and survival.
key_sub: Temperature, water, light, soil and salt decide what can live in a habitat.
body_html:
How to think about it

The physical conditions of a habitat are its non-living parts: temperature, water, light, soil, salt and oxygen.

  • Each living thing grows best in a certain range of conditions.
  • When conditions change (drought, flood, heatwave, salinity, bushfire), some living things grow better and others struggle or die.
  • To test a condition, change only that condition and measure growth or survival.
Example

Coral turns white in a marine heatwave. Which condition changed?

the water stayed too warm

Answer: temperature

Example

Seedlings: 0 h light 2 cm, 8 h light 15 cm. Pattern?

height goes up as light goes up

Answer: more light, more growth

Common mistakes

  • Calling a living thing (such as predators or trees) a physical condition.
  • Thinking more water or light is always better (too much can harm).
  • Changing two conditions in one test.

faq.q: What are physical conditions in a habitat?
faq.a: They are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as temperature, water, light, soil, wind, salt and oxygen in the water.

faq.q: How does drought affect living things?
faq.a: During a drought, rivers and billabongs dry up and plants wilt. Animals that need water, such as frogs and fish, can die or move away.
When sea water stays too warm, corals push out the tiny algae that live inside them and give them colour and food. The coral turns white and may die.

items.q: A bushfire burns the canopy, so more sunlight reaches the ground. Which physical condition has changed?
items.e: Physical conditions are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as amount of light.

items.q: Which change in a creek would most harm fish?
c: more shade on a hot day
items.e: Fish need oxygen dissolved in the water.

items.q: Why do fewer plants grow under a big gum tree than in the open field?
c: Less light reaches the ground under the tree.
items.e: Plants need light to make food.

items.q: Which of these is a physical (non-living) condition of a habitat?
items.e: Physical conditions include temperature, water, light, soil and salt. Living things are not physical conditions.

items.q: How can a long drought affect frogs in a billabong?
c: The water dries up, so frogs cannot breed and many die.
items.e: Water is a key physical condition.

items.q: A dam is built and the river below it gets colder water. Which physical condition has changed?
c: amount of oxygen in the water
items.e: Physical conditions are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as temperature.

items.q: After a bushfire, more sunlight reaches the forest floor. What happens next?
c: The trees grow back in one day.
No plants can ever grow again.
Many seedlings sprout and grow quickly.
items.e: Many Australian plants regrow after fire.

items.q: A hot summer heats the shallow water over a coral reef. Which physical condition has changed?
c: amount of oxygen in the water
items.e: Physical conditions are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as temperature.

items.q: The tide comes in twice a day over the mangrove mud. Which physical condition has changed?
c: amount of oxygen in the water
items.e: Physical conditions are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as amount of salt (salinity).

items.q: Organisms in a community depend on each other. Which is an example?
c: A rock gives shelter to a fish.
Bees get nectar from flowers and help to pollinate them.
items.e: Both organisms are living.

items.q: What happens to many coral when the water stays too hot for weeks?
c: They lose their colourful algae and turn white (bleaching).
They turn into rock straight away.
items.e: Bleached corals may die if the heat lasts.

items.q: Which of these is a physical (non-living) condition of a habitat?
c: the amount of grass eaten by sheep
items.e: Physical conditions include temperature, water, light, soil and salt. Living things are not physical conditions.

items.q: Which change would most likely cause the population of guppies in a pond to decrease?
c: The pond becomes polluted with oil.
More water plants grow in the pond.
items.e: Oil stops oxygen from entering the water.

items.q: Water plants such as Hydrilla help fish in a pond. How?
c: They give out oxygen when they make food in light.
items.e: Fish need oxygen dissolved in the water.

items.q: Floods cover a red gum forest for several months. Which physical condition has changed?
c: amount of oxygen in the water
items.e: Physical conditions are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as amount of water.

items.q: Clay soil stays waterlogged after rain. Which physical condition has changed?
c: amount of oxygen in the water
items.e: Physical conditions are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as type of soil.

items.q: Which list contains only physical conditions?
items.e: Physical conditions are non-living.

items.q: Sandy soil in the desert holds very little water. Which physical condition has changed?
items.e: Physical conditions are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as type of soil.

items.q: Ferns grow well under tall trees in a forest. Which factor most likely helps them grow there?
items.e: Many ferns grow well in shady, damp places.

items.q: Which of these is a physical (non-living) condition of a habitat?
items.e: Physical conditions include temperature, water, light, soil and salt. Living things are not physical conditions.

items.q: Why does a bean plant grown in a dark cupboard become pale and thin?
c: Cupboards are too cold for all plants.
It does not get enough light to make food.
items.e: Plants need light to make their food.

items.q: Which physical conditions best describe a mangrove swamp?
c: fresh, still water that may dry up in summer
salty, muddy and covered by tides
warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight
items.e: A mangrove swamp: salty, muddy and covered by tides.

items.q: How is a grey mangrove suited to salty, muddy shores?
c: Its large fronds catch the little light on the forest floor.
Its grey, hairy leaves reflect heat and it copes with salt.
Its leaves get rid of salt and its roots poke up to take in air.
It rests in the shade by day and needs little water.
items.e: Its features suit these physical conditions.

items.q: Which conditions does a hard coral survive best in?
items.e: Tiny algae inside it need sunlight to make food.

items.q: What is a habitat?
c: the place where a living thing lives and finds what it needs
a group of the same animals
items.e: It provides food, water, shelter and the right conditions.

items.q: Which conditions does a saltbush survive best in?
items.e: Its grey, hairy leaves reflect heat and it copes with salt.

items.q: Which living thing is best suited to a tropical rainforest (warm, wet and shady near the ground)?
items.e: Its features suit these conditions.

items.q: Which conditions does a tree fern survive best in?
items.e: Its large fronds catch the little light on the forest floor.

items.q: Which living thing is best suited to a cool temperate forest in Tasmania (cool, wet and shaded)?
items.e: Its features suit these conditions.

items.q: How is a mountain pygmy possum suited to alpine boulder fields?
c: Its skin channels dew and rain to its mouth.
Tiny algae inside it need sunlight to make food.
Its grey, hairy leaves reflect heat and it copes with salt.
It hibernates under the snow in winter.
items.e: Its features suit these physical conditions.

items.q: Why do mangroves grow on muddy shores but gum trees do not?
c: Mangroves can cope with salty water and waterlogged mud.
Mud is too hot for gum trees.
Gum trees grow only in snow.
items.e: Each plant suits certain conditions.

items.q: Which physical conditions best describe the Great Barrier Reef?
c: very hot days, cold nights and little water
warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight
warm, wet and shady near the ground
items.e: The Great Barrier Reef: warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight.

items.q: Which conditions does a snow gum survive best in?
items.e: It can survive frost and snow and regrows after fire.

items.q: How is a thorny devil suited to the hot, dry outback?
c: Its skin channels dew and rain to its mouth.
Its grey, hairy leaves reflect heat and it copes with salt.
Tiny algae inside it need sunlight to make food.
It can survive frost and snow and regrows after fire.
items.e: Its features suit these physical conditions.

items.q: Which living thing is best suited to a sandy beach (salty wind, loose sand and strong sun)?
items.e: Its features suit these conditions.

items.q: How is a water-holding frog suited to dry inland claypans?
c: It burrows and seals itself in a cocoon until rain returns.
Tiny algae inside it need sunlight to make food.
It can survive frost and snow and regrows after fire.
It rests in the shade by day and needs little water.
items.e: Its features suit these physical conditions.

items.q: Which physical conditions best describe a cool temperate forest in Tasmania?
c: warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight
cold, windy and snowy in winter
warm, wet and shady near the ground
items.e: A cool temperate forest in Tasmania: cool, wet and shaded.

items.q: Which living thing is best suited to the Great Barrier Reef (warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight)?
items.e: Its features suit these conditions.

items.q: Which physical conditions best describe the Australian Alps?
c: warm, wet and shady near the ground
very hot days, cold nights and little water
cold, windy and snowy in winter
warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight
items.e: The Australian Alps: cold, windy and snowy in winter.

items.q: Which conditions does a thorny devil survive best in?
items.e: Its skin channels dew and rain to its mouth.

items.q: Harper wonders: what would happen to a cactus moved to a wet swamp?
c: It would change its body right away to fit in.
It would not survive well. Its roots would get too much water and rot.
items.e: Its roots would get too much water and rot.

items.q: Why do the same plants not grow in Darwin and in Hobart?
c: Plants only grow in capital cities.
The temperature and rainfall are very different.
items.e: Climate sets the conditions of a habitat.

items.q: Which conditions does a grey mangrove survive best in?
items.e: Its leaves get rid of salt and its roots poke up to take in air.

items.q: Which habitat would most likely have the largest community?
c: a large forest with many kinds of plants and animals
items.e: More food and shelter supports more populations.

items.q: Why do few plants grow in salty farm paddocks?
c: Salt makes the soil too cold.
Too much salt makes it hard for roots to take in water.
items.e: Salinity is a problem in parts of the Murray-Darling Basin.

items.q: Mangrove trees give shelter to crabs and mudskippers. What does this show?
c: Crabs make food for the trees.
Organisms in a community depend on each other.
items.e: Plants give animals food and shelter.

items.q: How is a river red gum suited to inland riverbanks that flood?
c: Its seeds sprout after floods and its roots survive wet soil.
It rests in the shade by day and needs little water.
Tiny algae inside it need sunlight to make food.
Its skin channels dew and rain to its mouth.
items.e: Its features suit these physical conditions.

items.q: An oil spill covered a mangrove swamp. Which statement is most likely true?
c: Only the trees would be affected.
Many populations in the community would decrease.
items.e: Organisms in a community depend on each other.

items.q: Inland rivers dry up during a long drought. Which physical condition has changed?
c: amount of oxygen in the water
items.e: Physical conditions are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as amount of water.

items.q: How is a red kangaroo suited to dry inland grasslands?
c: It hibernates under the snow in winter.
It rests in the shade by day and needs little water.
Its leaves get rid of salt and its roots poke up to take in air.
Its skin channels dew and rain to its mouth.
items.e: Its features suit these physical conditions.

items.q: Why does a pond community have more snails when there are more water plants?
c: The snails make their own food.
items.e: Snails feed on water plants and algae.

items.q: Mia counted 5 kinds of animals and 3 kinds of plants in a garden. How many populations are there in the community?
items.e: Each kind of plant and animal is one population.

items.q: Harper wonders: what would happen to a fern moved to a sunny desert?
c: It would not survive well. It needs shade and damp soil.
It would change its body right away to fit in.
items.e: It needs shade and damp soil.

items.q: William wonders: what would happen to a sea turtle moved to a desert?
c: It would not survive well. It needs the ocean for food and swimming.
It would change its body right away to fit in.
items.e: It needs the ocean for food and swimming.

items.q: Algae grow in a still creek and use up the oxygen at night. Which physical condition has changed?
c: amount of oxygen in the water
items.e: Physical conditions are the non-living parts of a habitat, such as amount of oxygen in the water.

items.q: A gardener cleared all the dead leaves from under a tree. What would most likely happen to the millipedes living there?
c: Their population decreases because they lose food and shelter.
items.e: Millipedes feed on and shelter in dead leaves.

items.q: Chloe wonders: what would happen to a goldfish moved to a dry field?
c: It would not survive well. It needs water to breathe with its gills.
It would change its body right away to fit in.
items.e: It needs water to breathe with its gills.

items.q: Aarav wants to find out if earthworms prefer damp or dry soil. Which must he keep the same on both sides?
c: the amount of water in the soil
the number of earthworms that move
the amount of light and the type of soil
items.e: Only the factor tested may change.

items.q: Which conditions does a river red gum survive best in?
items.e: Its seeds sprout after floods and its roots survive wet soil.

items.q: Matilda counted 40 guppies in a pond in January and 12 in June. The pond became very shallow in June. What is the best explanation?
c: There was less water and less space, so fewer guppies survived.
More food grew in the pond.
items.e: A change in a habitat affects the population.

items.q: Which physical conditions best describe the outback desert?
c: very hot days, cold nights and little water
fresh, still water that may dry up in summer
cold, windy and snowy in winter
warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight
items.e: The outback desert: very hot days, cold nights and little water.

items.q: A pond had many water plants. After they were removed, the fish swam near the surface. Why?
c: There was more food at the surface.
There was less oxygen in the water.
items.e: Water plants add oxygen to the water.

items.q: Which living thing is best suited to the outback desert (very hot days, cold nights and little water)?
items.e: Its features suit these conditions.

items.q: Which living thing is best suited to a mangrove swamp (salty, muddy and covered by tides)?
items.e: Its features suit these conditions.

items.q: Which physical conditions best describe a freshwater billabong?
c: warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight
salty wind, loose sand and strong sun
warm, wet and shady near the ground
fresh, still water that may dry up in summer
items.e: A freshwater billabong: fresh, still water that may dry up in summer.

items.q: Which tool measures rainfall in a habitat?
items.e: Rainfall is measured in millimetres.

items.q: Liam grows grass seeds in sand and in soil. The soil grass grows much better. What can he conclude?
c: Grass survives better in soil than in sand.
Seeds don't need soil or sand.
items.e: Some places fit a plant better.

items.q: Which physical conditions best describe a sandy beach?
c: salty wind, loose sand and strong sun
warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight
fresh, still water that may dry up in summer
very hot days, cold nights and little water
items.e: A sandy beach: salty wind, loose sand and strong sun.

items.q: Which tool would Kai use to measure how much light reaches the forest floor?
items.e: Light meters measure brightness.

items.q: In Mia's cress test, what should she measure?
c: the number of seeds that sprout each day
items.e: Measure the result of the change.

items.q: Ella grows two sets of seedlings with the same soil, water and light, but one set is watered with salty water. What is she testing?
items.e: Only the salt changes.

items.q: A desert gets much more rain for many years. Which plants might start to grow well there?
items.e: When a habitat changes, which living things survive well can change.

items.q: Which living thing is best suited to a freshwater billabong (fresh, still water that may dry up in summer)?
items.e: Its features suit these conditions.

items.q: Mia wants to know which habitat is best for a tadpole. Where should she test it?
items.e: Tadpoles need water.

items.q: Ruby measures soil temperature in the sun (38 °C) and under a tree (24 °C). Which living thing is more likely to survive under the tree?
c: a worm that dries out in heat
items.e: Shade keeps soil cooler and damper.

items.q: Which physical conditions best describe a tropical rainforest?
c: very hot days, cold nights and little water
cold, windy and snowy in winter
warm, clear, salty water with lots of sunlight
warm, wet and shady near the ground
items.e: A tropical rainforest: warm, wet and shady near the ground.

items.q: Jack counts slaters under logs in a dry area (4) and a damp area (31). What does this suggest?
c: Slaters do not live under logs.
items.e: The big difference suggests a pattern; repeating would check it.

items.q: A scientist finds fewer platypus in a river after a dam is built. Which condition should she measure first?
c: the water temperature and flow below the dam
the height of the dam wall
items.e: Dams change the physical conditions downstream.

items.q: Priya puts slaters in a box with a wet side and a dry side. After 10 minutes, most are on the wet side. What does this show?
c: Slaters survive better in damp places.
items.e: Their choice shows the habitat they need.

items.q: Mia wants to test whether temperature affects how fast cress seeds sprout. What should she change?
items.e: Change only the temperature.
